source.title: Unveiling Multiple Descents in Unsupervised Autoencoders
source.authors: Kobi Rahimi; Yehonathan Refael; Tom Tirer; Ofir Lindenbaum

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted graphics are garbled in the text extraction, so their curve values cannot be read numerically.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests double-descent behavior in unsupervised autoencoders using reconstruction loss, rather than the original supervised settings. It reports model-, epoch-, and sample-wise sweeps and results about when descents appear.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-loss results for model size, epochs, and sample count, including text-described trends and curves. Rows below cover those results and the stated linear-AE comparison. Downstream-task metrics, training-loss-only findings, and cited results are not recorded as rows because they do not measure the claim versions’ test-error behavior.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-loss curves for unsupervised autoencoders (AEs) trained on contaminated data and tested on clean data. It sweeps model size, epochs and sample count. This is a new setting (unsupervised reconstruction rather than supervised prediction) aimed at whether model-, epoch- and sample-wise double descent occur, and what noise does to them.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors show analytically and empirically that linear AEs lack double descent. They report that nonlinear AEs show model-, epoch- and sample-wise double or triple descent under strong contamination (noise, low SNR, shifts, anomalies), with bottleneck size shaping the curve. They also claim over-parameterized AEs improve downstream anomaly detection and domain adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses unsupervised autoencoders trained to reconstruct contaminated inputs and evaluated mainly on clean data, rather than the original supervised prediction setups. It varies bottleneck/hidden dimensions, training epochs, and sample count.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior depends on nonlinearity, bottleneck and hidden-layer dimensions, sample/feature noise proportion, SNR, domain shift, dataset, and architecture. Low noise or low shifts can remove or weaken the descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream ROC-AUC (anomaly detection) and KNN-DAT domain mixing are non-monotonic in model size. Critical-regime models do worst; on CelebA this happens even without test-loss double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent in reconstruction loss carries over to non-monotonic downstream-task performance in unsupervised models.

record.problems: Many test-loss results are presented in figures without recoverable numerical values in the supplied text. The experiments use datasets of moderate size, which the authors attribute to computational constraints. The study evaluates a restricted set of autoencoder architectures and contamination settings; there is no tuned-regularization comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version test-loss rows omitted. Training-loss-only curves and downstream anomaly-detection or domain-adaptation metrics were excluded because they do not measure the test-error outcomes specified by these versions.

untested.parts: No non-network model classes are tested, beyond the linear AE.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested. Noise is said to shift the critical regime to larger models, but this is not quantified against any measure.
Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
There is no re-plot against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Heatmap of nonlinear AE test loss over hidden and bottleneck sizes. It shows bottleneck-wise and hidden-wise double descent, with the critical regime shifting as the bottleneck grows.
Synthetic anomaly contamination: double descent in clean test loss at low SAR with many anomalies, none at SAR 0 dB.
Real domain shift on single-cell RNA, with triple descent on the Wang target; MNIST to MNIST-M and the reverse with CNNs.
CIFAR-10 CNN model-wise double descent across sample noise and SNR.
Feature-noise results: the peak shifts left with more noisy features, and more feature noise lowers test loss on RNA.
Final ascent (fall-rise-fall-rise) under extreme noise; Laplacian noise; sparse AEs.
CNN and nonlinear-subspace epoch-wise and sample-wise double descent, and epoch-wise descent under domain shift.

record.verdict_notes: Test loss is reconstruction error on clean data after training on contaminated data, which is an analogue of training on noisy labels. Most curves are only readable from the figures. 'Non-monotonic' is sometimes used where a clear double descent isn't asserted. V4 rows were restricted to the linear-AE model class, because nonlinear AEs are deep networks and bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: Tested in autoencoders under the paper’s contamination and data settings; not an evaluation across deep-network families generally.
Tested for the reported autoencoder architectures and contamination settings; not across other training procedures or model families.
Tested for selected autoencoder/data settings; not established as a general effect across models or datasets.
Multiple AE architectures are tested, but the study does not test the general curve across model classes beyond autoencoders.
The paper discusses bottleneck size and layer dimensions, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Noise dependence and double/triple descents are tested. The effect of optimally tuned regularization on eliminating peaks is not tested.

The paper discusses parameter allocation and bottleneck dimensions, but does not measure the curves against an appropriate effective parameter count or show that second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.
